common_name: Peter's Honey Fig (Small Yellow-Green Sweet Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; figs are self-fertile and need no pollinator. Peter's Honey fruits on both old wood (breba crop) and new growth (main crop), giving two harvest windows in zone 9.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate poor soil but grow and fruit best with consistent moisture during fruit development. Peter's Honey is a fig cultivar collected and popularized among southern fig enthusiasts for its small-to-medium, pale yellow-green fruit with a honeyed, richly sweet flavor that belies its modest size and unassuming skin color. The tree is productive and vigorous, producing a light breba crop on overwintered wood in early summer followed by a heavier main crop on new growth from midsummer into fall. Because the fruit does not need to color up to signal ripeness, harvest by feel — ripe figs soften and the neck droops — rather than by color change. Prune in late winter to control size and remove any winter-killed tips, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system through Gulf Coast summers.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Fig Cultivars for Louisiana

common_name: Beall Fig (Heirloom Gulf South Bronze Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; figs are self-fertile and need no pollinator. Beall is an old Gulf South heirloom fig, passed down and shared among home growers for generations rather than commercially released.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; figs tolerate a wide range of soils but produce their best fruit with consistent moisture during ripening. Beall is a long-passed-down heirloom fig from the Gulf South, maintained by home orchardists and fig collectors rather than through commercial nursery release, producing medium bronze-brown fruit with sweet, richly flavored, pink-to-amber flesh. Like most Gulf Coast heirloom figs, it is valued for its vigor and reliability under regional heat and humidity, ripening over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to control size and remove winter dieback, and mulch well to protect the shallow root system; established Beall trees tolerate the occasional hard freeze common to zone 8-9 winters, resprouting from the base if top growth is killed back.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Fig Cultivars for Louisiana

common_name: Texas Blue Giant Fig (Large Purple-Black Texas Fig)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring; figs are self-fertile and need no pollinator. Texas Blue Giant produces very large fruit on vigorous growth, so give it plenty of room and rich soil for the best fruit size.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; figs benefit from consistent moisture during the fruiting season to size fruit well and avoid splitting. Texas Blue Giant is a large-fruited fig popular among Texas and Gulf South fig growers, producing sizeable, deep purple-black fruit with sweet, richly flavored strawberry-red flesh on a vigorous, spreading tree. Its large fruit size and dark, attractive skin color make it a favorite for fresh eating and preserving, and the tree is well adapted to regional heat and humidity, cropping over an extended midsummer-to-fall season. Prune in late winter to manage its vigorous size and remove any winter dieback, and mulch heavily to protect the shallow root system through summer heat and occasional winter cold snaps.

common_name: Pisang Raja Banana (Southeast Asian Dessert Banana)

planting.note: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pisang Raja is a true tropical banana with little cold tolerance, so in zone 9 grow it in the warmest, most protected microclimate available and expect it to freeze back most winters.

directions: Plant divisions (pups) after last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, feeding heavily through the growing season since bananas are gross feeders. Pisang Raja, meaning 'king banana' in Malay and Indonesian, is one of the most widely grown and highly regarded dessert bananas in Southeast Asia, prized for its dense, creamy, richly aromatic flesh with a distinctive honeyed flavor that many consider superior to Cavendish-type bananas for fresh eating. The moderately sized fruits have thick yellow skin with characteristic black spotting when fully ripe. In zone 9a, where winter freezes routinely kill the pseudostem to the ground, treat it as a root-hardy perennial: mulch heavily over winter and expect regrowth from the rhizome in spring, though a freeze-free run of 12-15 months is typically needed to reach fruiting size, so a large container that can be moved to shelter improves the odds of a crop.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Banana Cultivars
California Rare Fruit Growers Association — Banana Variety Notes
